title: Effective Contact Theory for Exotic Loosely Bound States in Strongly Interacting Expanding Matter
authors: Xiaofeng Wang, Zebo Tang, Zhangbu Xu, Chi Yang, Wangmei Zha
abstract: Short-distance correlations generate universal relations that can be independent of microscopic details. Tan's contact is a prominent example, connecting close pairs, high-momentum constituents, and bound-state formation across atomic, condensed-matter, and nuclear systems. Whether an analogous universality governs the nonequilibrium freeze-out of relativistic QCD matter is an open question. We develop an effective contact theory that relates the production of loosely bound states to continuum two-particle correlations in heavy-ion collisions. The construction replaces the hard relative-momentum cutoff of conventional coalescence by a regulated Bethe--Peierls kernel: freeze-out localization fixes its momentum scale, while the composite yield fixes its contact residue. Bound and continuum observables then become projections of a common two-particle density matrix rather than independent phenomena. Coulomb-bound $Kμ$ atoms provide an ideal realization because their atomic, production, and source scales are widely separated. A contact-theory analysis of STAR $dΛ$ correlations supplies a first bound--continuum consistency test and demonstrates how inferred near-threshold parameters can depend on the finite expanding source. The framework establishes a general strategy for relating coalescence, correlations, and exotic bound states in strongly interacting expanding matter.
summary: This work introduces an effective contact theory to unify the description of exotic bound states (like Kmu atoms) and continuum particle correlations in the extreme environment of heavy-ion collisions. By replacing sharp cutoffs with a regulated kernel, the theory posits that both observables stem from a single underlying two-particle density matrix. This establishes a powerful, general methodology for analyzing strongly interacting, expanding matter.
main_problem: The paper develops a theory to relate the production of loosely bound states to continuum two-particle correlations in strongly interacting, expanding matter, addressing the challenge of scale separation.
main_result: The effective contact theory unifies bound and continuum observables as projections of a common two-particle density matrix, providing a general framework for coalescence and correlation studies.
method: It replaces the hard momentum cutoff of conventional coalescence models with a regulated Bethe-Peierls kernel, derived from an effective contact theory based on Tan's universal relations.
model_or_system: The study uses relativistic heavy-ion collisions (like STAR) as the physical laboratory, focusing specifically on the analysis of Coulomb-bound Kmu atoms.
key_observables: Atom yield, two-particle correlations (e.g., STAR dLambda correlations), and the common two-particle density matrix.
important_parameters: Localization momentum scale ($p_0$), source scale ($\Lambda_{fo}$), and the effective contact residue ($C$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that bound and continuum populations originate from projections of a single, common two-particle density matrix at freeze-out.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general concept of Tan's contact to develop the effective theory, applying it first to the idealized case of Kmu atoms, and finally testing the framework using continuum correlation data from heavy-ion collisions.
why_interesting: The concept of relating bound states and continuum correlations via a universal contact term is highly relevant to non-equilibrium many-body physics, echoing ideas used in quantum optics and open quantum systems where short-range interactions dominate.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Comparison of the published STAR dΛ correlations in three centrality classes. Black points are the STAR data [30]. Red solid curves are continuous evaluations of the common-γ contact fit in Eq. (44); blue dashed curves are continuous evaluations of an independently fitted analytic LL benchmark. Purple dash-dotted curves are STAR’s published acceptance-folded LL best fits. The benchmark radii are (3.31, 2.98, 2.56) fm, whereas STAR reports (2.69 ± 0.20, 2.44 ± 0.17, 2.08 ± 0.19) fm. The difference between the two LL curves exposes sensitivity to the source radii, scattering parameters, effective ranges, and implementation.
